item.title: Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims Report
item.description: In the week ending November 21, the advance figure for seasonally adjusted initial claims was 189,000, a decrease of 13,000 from the previous week's revised level. item.title: US Department of Labor proposes to update fiduciary rule to affirm Employee Retirement Income Security Act’s exclusive purpose rule
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration today issued proposed amendments to the investment duties regulation to clarify the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.The proposed rule seeks to end the 32-year uncertainty surrounding whether ERISA allows fiduciaries to consider non-financial factors in retirement plan investments, including environmental, social, and governance, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. The proposal gives fiduciaries an affirmative expression of their duty of loyalty, which would clarify that ERISA requires plan fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing for the interests of participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.“President Trump’s Department of Labor is not putting its thumb on the scale for or against any particular investment or asset class,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas. Our focus is on protecting and growing Americans’ retirement savings, which have reached record levels thanks to President Trump.”If finalized, the proposal would also place a heightened focus on shareholder engagement and proxy voting by fiduciaries to secure the retirement interests of American workers and would avoid the improper pressures and influence placed on plan fiduciaries. This includes voting shares and otherwise attempting to influence corporate behavior through shareholder engagement activities for ESG/DEI purposes. The proposed rule follows the directive in President Trump’s executive order, “Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors,” which instructed the department to strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA.“President Trump has directed the department to assess whether certain proxy advisor firms spreading ESG and DEI are acting solely in the financial interest of plan participants,” said Assistant Secretary for the Employee Benefits Security Administration Daniel Aronowitz. “Our proposed rule does just that by making clear what is, and what isn’t, loyal behavior when it comes to proxy voting and shareholder engagement.” The proposal would remove two departmental inventions that are not consistent with ERISA and may be misused by fiduciaries with ulterior motives – the tiebreaker test and the participant preference provision. Under the tiebreaker test, a fiduciary can say that two investments are “equal” and then pick their preferred investment, which may include ESG funds. Similarly, fiduciaries can elicit the views of participants who support ESG investments and use that as a pretext to permit investments they otherwise would not be allowed to include under federal retirement laws. The proposed rule will be published in the Nov. 24 edition of the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days after its publication.EBSA ensures the security of retirement, health, and other job-based benefits for American workers and their families. The agency is responsible for protecting more than 155 million workers, retirees, and their families, who are covered by approximately 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 private retirement plans, and 521,000 additional welfare benefit plans. Together, these plans hold about $15.2 trillion in assets.Employers and workers can contact EBSA at askebsa.dol.gov or call 866-444-3272 toll-free for help with private sector job-based retirement and health plans.Read the notice of proposed rulemaking on Loyalty and the Exclusive Purpose Rule in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights.

item.title: US Department of Labor announces final rule clarifying employee, independent contractor status under federal wage and hour laws
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. The new final rule provides clarity to businesses and workers alike, as well as the division’s enforcement personnel.U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Wage and Hour Division Administrator Andrew Rogers, and other department officials hosted an event to formally announce the final rule at the Frances Perkins Building this morning. Employers, business associations, worker advocates, independent contractors, and other stakeholders were in attendance as Secretary Sonderling highlighted the clarity and simplicity of the new regulations.The final rule rescinds an earlier 2024 rule addressing the classification of employees and independent contractors and replaces it with an analysis that is substantially similar to the framework adopted by the department in 2021. Consistent with the outcomes of federal appellate cases, the final rule provides further guidance on the process for differentiating between employees with protections under the FLSA and individuals who work as independent contractors.“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” said Secretary Sonderling. “The new Independent Contractor final rule establishes clear, predictable, and easy-to-understand criteria for determining who is an employee and who is an independent contractor – allowing millions of Americans to take advantage of new opportunities in President Trump’s booming economy.”The final rule also applies the department’s streamlined analysis to the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, both of which use the FLSA’s statutory definition of “employ.” However, the rule does not change the assessment of employee or independent contractor status for the purpose of any other federal laws, including the Internal Revenue Code, and does not preempt any state or local laws.“The Department of Labor is committed to helping employers prevent misclassification. This rule strikes the right balance by protecting employees who are entitled to the protections of federal wage and hour laws, while also respecting the entrepreneurial spirit of legitimate independent contractors,” said Administrator Rogers. “The department distilled longstanding judicial tests into a framework that employees and employers can reliably apply at the outset of business relationships.”The analysis in the department’s final rule does the following:Applies an “economic reality” test to determine whether a worker is in business for himself or herself as an independent contractor or is an employee economically dependent on an employer for work.Identifies and explains two “core factors” to help determine if a worker is economically dependent on an employer for work or in business for himself or herself:The nature and degree of control over the work.The worker’s opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative and/or investment.Identifies other factors to help determine a worker’s status as an employee or independent contractor, including the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.Advises that the actual practice of the worker and the potential employer is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible.Provides 14 fact-specific examples applying the factors to real-life circumstances. The department published a notice of proposed rulemaking on Feb. 27, 2026, and received approximately 16,500 public comments during a 60-day comment period. After reviewing this feedback, the department finalized the rule with modifications and enhancements. For example, in response to commenter requests, the final rule includes new illustrative examples involving farm labor contractors, digital platform workers, and truck drivers.Workers and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the FMLA.WATCH the Independent Contractor Final Rule Announcement.Read Secretary Sonderling’s Op-Ed on the Final Rule.Read the final rule, which takes effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

item.title: US Department of Labor obtains court order requiring NJ-based construction contractor to pay $2.2M in back wages, damages, penalties
item.description: ENGLEWOOD CLIFFS, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a construction contractor to pay more than $2 million in back wages and damages to 323 construction workers.     Entered Nov. 16, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, the consent judgment resolves the department’s litigation alleging Premier Concrete Systems LLC and its owners, Peter Tiflinsky and Antonio Escada, violated overtime and recordkeeping provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.The litigation was a result of an investigation by the department’s Wage and Hour Division that found the company and its owners paid employees cash at straight-time rates for all hours worked and failed to pay them time and one-half their regular rate of pay for hours over 40 in a workweek as required by the FLSA. “Construction workers play a critical role across the country in ensuring safe and reliable structures. The Wage and Hour Division is committed to ensuring that construction workers are paid in compliance with federal labor laws,” said Wage and Hour Division Regional Administrator James Cain in Philadelphia.The judgment requires Premier Concrete Systems to pay 323 employees back wages totaling $1,040,648 and an equal amount in damages. The judgment also requires the defendants to pay a civil penalty of $118,704 and prohibits defendants from violating the FLSA in the future.“The resolution of this case is a clear reminder for employers in the construction industry to remember their responsibilities under the law,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. Rogoff in New York City.Employees and employers can contact the division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division.The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential FLSA minimum wage and overtime violations, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including a search tool that workers can use if they think they may be owed back wages collected by the division. Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

item.title: US Department of Labor issues opinion letters addressing Fair Labor Standards Act exemption, Family and Medical Leave Act hours of service
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today issued two opinion letters that address real-world questions related to the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Family and Medical Leave Act.The two opinion letters address the applicability of the exemption for amusement and recreational establishments under the Fair Labor Standards Act and the hours-of-service requirement under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Opinion letters provide official written interpretations from the department’s Wage and Hour Division that explain how the laws that the department enforces apply to specific factual circumstances and may help the public understand their rights and responsibilities. The division is committed to providing opinion letters that help American workers and businesses understand how the FLSA and FMLA apply to their situations.   The two opinion letters issued today are:FLSA2026-14: Whether the exemption for seasonal amusement and recreational establishments in section 13(a)(3) of the FLSA applies to a concessionaire that provides food and drinks at events such as a state fair and concerts.FMLA2026-3: Whether time spent writing mandatory reports outside of scheduled work hours and traveling between worksites counts as hours of service under the FMLA. In 2025, the department announced the relaunch of the opinion letter program, which expands its longstanding commitment to providing meaningful compliance assistance that helps workers, employers, and other stakeholders understand how federal labor laws apply in specific workplace circumstances.Visit the Wage and Hour Division’s opinion letters page to explore past guidance and find information on how to submit a request for an opinion letter.Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the FMLA.Read opinion letters FLSA2026-14 and FMLA2026-3.

item.title: US Department of Labor proposes new class exemption for qualified professional asset managers to protect retirement plans from disruptions
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration today proposed a class exemption that would streamline the process for qualified professional asset managers to continue engaging in transactions permitted under Prohibited Transaction Class Exemption 84-14 – also known as the QPAM exemption – following an ineligibility event. The proposed QPAM Re-eligibility Options After Disqualification Class Exemption, known as QROAD, contains safeguards to protect plans and participants through clear, well-established conditions, including the requirement that asset managers seeking relief under the proposed exemption have an independent fiduciary certify their eligibility and compliance.“For years, QPAMs seeking to rely on the beneficial QPAM class exemption following an ineligibility event have had to go through an individual exemption process that can be costly, burdensome, and time-consuming for everyone involved,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “The QROAD class exemption addresses that problem by creating an alternative path to relief while maintaining the high standards of integrity needed to protect affected plans and participants.”Since 1984, the QPAM exemption has provided broad relief for employee benefit plan and IRA transactions that otherwise would be prohibited under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act if the transactions involved a qualified professional asset manager. QPAMs are expected to maintain a high standard of integrity. If the QPAM or certain of its related parties engage in ineligibility events, such as a criminal conviction or prohibited misconduct, it cannot rely on the QPAM exemption for 10 years. The department has granted several individual exemptions over the years that allow QPAMs to continue to rely on the QPAM exemption notwithstanding such disqualification. For such exemptions, QPAMs must demonstrate that their continued reliance on the QPAM exemption would protect and benefit plans and their participants and beneficiaries. Without this exemptive relief, plans could be forced to unwind investments or replace their asset managers.  These costly disruptions can reduce plan assets and participants’ retirement savings. Comments on the proposed class exemption are due 60 days from its publication in the Federal Register. Read the proposed QROAD class exemption and fact sheet to learn more.

item.title: US Department of Labor cites powder coating company for willful toxic substance exposures, repeat violations, proposes more than $1.6M in penalties
item.description: HOUSTON – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a powder coating and furniture restoration company for willfully and repeatedly exposing workers to toxic substances and other safety and health hazards.The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration conducted three inspections of Outdoor Furniture Refinishing Inc. – doing business as Allied Powder Coating – on April 10, 2026. One inspection addressed complaint items after the employer provided an inadequate response to an inquiry, and two follow-up inspections were initiated in relation to safety and health violations found during a December 2023 inspection. The employer’s failure to submit abatement documentation prompted a comprehensive review of ongoing hazards.OSHA cited the company for three willful violations for exposing workers to hazardous levels of 1,3,5-triglycidyl isocyanurate and total dust during powder coating operations. The agency also issued 18 serious violations for failing to provide training on excessive noise exposure and for deficiencies involving respiratory protection, hazard communication, personal protective equipment, forklift operations, electrical safety, and portable ladders.In addition, OSHA cited the company for 18 repeat violations related to respiratory protection, noise overexposure, spray booths, hazard communication, compressed air, and electrical hazards. The agency also issued one other-than-serious violation for unsanitary working conditions.OSHA has proposed $1,640,888 in penalties.The agency found that, despite multiple inspections since 2013 and a formal settlement agreement finalized in December 2024, the company has failed to take meaningful action to correct recurring violations.The employer has 15 business days from receipt of its citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.Learn more about OSHA, and protecting workers from the hazards of abrasive blasting. Employers can also contact the agency for information about OSHA’s compliance assistance resources and for free help on complying with OSHA standards.

item.title: US Department of Labor proposes to modernize permanent labor certification recruitment, strengthening protections for American workers
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today issued a proposed rule that would enhance American worker protections when employers apply for certification to hire foreign workers permanently in the United States. The proposed rule modernizes the Permanent Labor Certification program by strengthening recruitment standards and recordkeeping requirements, eliminating administrative exemptions to the statutory labor market test, and improving safeguards for all American workers, especially those affected by layoffs. This proposed update to the PERM program – the first comprehensive set of regulatory reforms to the program in nearly 20 years – will ensure that highly qualified American workers receive fair consideration and first access to job opportunities.“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.”The proposed rule would require employers to level the playing field when recruiting workers by using the same channels and methods when advertising jobs. Proposed changes include a requirement to replace print-based job advertisements with online recruiting through employer websites, online job boards, social media, job fairs, and campus recruitment. Employers would also be required to advertise positions for at least 90 calendar days and demonstrate that they made good-faith efforts to recruit qualified American workers. Under the proposal, employers would be prohibited from tailoring job opportunities to foreign workers. The department also proposed to eliminate the administrative exemption employers used to bypass the statutory labor market test for certain occupations. Under the proposal, employers recruiting for physical therapists, nurses, and workers with exceptional abilities in the sciences or arts would be required to consider qualified U.S. workers. The proposed rule also protects qualified American workers affected by layoffs by requiring ongoing consideration of laid off workers throughout the labor certification and immigrant petition processes, and prohibiting certain employers that have laid off American workers within the last 2 years from seeking permanent labor certification for the same or similar positions. Comments on the proposed rule are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. Additional information is available on ETA’s Office of Foreign Labor Certification website.
